chapter: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
title: Getting home from Georgia: the cab driver, baggage man and a woman's chicken
summary: His first time in the South, he was helped by a Black cab driver, a white baggage man and a woman on the train who shared food and a fish breakfast.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, what did you do?

Well, I'll tell you now what happened. I was standing there, and with my drums I didn't know where to go or how to move. I couldn't -- so a car passed by, I don't know what, but the lights shone on me, and when the lights shone I threw up my hands like this, and the guy stopped, and it was a colored cab driver. He said, "Boy what you doing out here this time of night? Good God almighty." That was my first time down south. I didn't know anything about the -- you know. So everything was just natural for me. You know, I didn't have any fears --
Oh, you didn't?
-- or any hangups. No, it was my first time. I didn't know anything about it. I thought it was just like being in Chicago or New York, to me.
Well, I'm glad you --
No, but I didn't, you know. I didn't feel anything. So this guy says -- I felt lonely because I wanted to get out of there.
Yeah.
Because I had my drums.
Yeah.
So he said, "Put your drums in the car,

kid. What are you doing out here? Let me get your out of here." So he took me to a colored restaurant, you know. And he said, "Are you hungry?" I said, "I have money." You know, because I had all my road money stacked up, a pocket full of money. So he said, "Get yourself something to eat." He said, "What are you going to do?" I said, "I'm trying to get home. I live in New York." He said, "Well, let's see --," it was about 2:00 o'clock in the morning, I guess, because we had finished about 12:30, 1:00 o'clock. The dance was over, so it was about 2:00, 2:30. So he said, "Well, you just set your drums in the hall and I'll come by and pick you up around 7:00. So you can sit here and play the phonograph."
They were open all night.
And entertain yourself. Yeah. Entertain yourself, and I'll come by and pick you up.
He was a nice guy, wasn't he?

Oh, wonderful, you know. So I sat around, you know, chewed the fat with the owner and told him about New York. He said, "New York. Oh, man, tell me about it." So I'd made a friend right there. Told him about Harlem, and --
Yeah.

And, oh, about 7:00 he came by. And the train was leaving about 8:15 that morning. It was going up through South Carolina, on up to Virginia, and then Baltimore, you know, that regular southern route, and then it goes up

through Philadelphia and the New York. So I had the presence of mind to check my drums through to New York. So when I went -- now this is funny -- when he took me to the train station, so there was, oh, an old white bagggge man, and when he heard my accent he was very nice. He saw I wasn't a southerner. So I said, "I'd like to check these through to New York." So he looked at me and said, "Well, we'll do just that." You know, I wasn't thinking like you're in the south, and I said, well, we'll check them through, "Pennsylvania Station would be good for me." And he said, "Now, I'll do just that." He checked my drums through and put them in the baggage car and everything, so I was free, you know. I said, well, when I get to New York my drums will be there. So he said, now, your ticket will be so and so and so and so, now you buy your ticket right here. So I bought my ticket and everything. Then he said, "Now, you wait here with me and I'll show you what car to get on." So I sat there with him and we talked.
You've got a big guardian angel sitting on top of you.

We sat there and talked. We laughed and talked about all kinds of things, you know. He was telling me jokes, you know, about a 'possum running through the trees, and this and that, and we laughed. This was my first time in the south. I hadn't been to the South in -- I hadn't been further south than Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and that was it.

Well, St. Louis, but I ain't calling it South, you know. So we sat there and laughed and talked and finally a train came, and he took me to the train. He said, "Get up there quick and get yourself that seat." So I jumped up and got myself a seat, and he says, "Okay, have a happy voyage." So as soon as I got on the train, and I got to somewhere in South Carolina. We went up through Georgia, up through that way, somewhere. But anyway, some woman got on the train, a young woman, I guess about in her 30s, had a basket of chicken, and you know how folks travelled in those days. So I was sitting over there alone. So she looked over at me. I just looked up in the air, you know, and looked away. So finally she said, "Would you like to share a little of this chicken with me?" So I said, "I really would, ma'am, thank you very much." So she gave me some chicken and biscuits. So this was around --
How amazing.

This was around 10:00 o'clock in the morning. So when the train gets to her home town, it stops for three hours. So she says, "When the train gets to here, it'll stop for three hours, but you can come over to my house and have breakfast." I went over to her house. Man, she put on a big fish dinner. Breakfast, what they called breakfast, you know, fried fish and all. And after I had eaten, she took me back to the train station and saw me off, and said, "'Bye-'Bye," and there I was, off for New York. Can you imagine that?
That was my experience in the South.
What color lady?
Yeah.
What color? A colored lady?
Yeah.
Gee whiz.
Then we went --
Well, she knew it was your first time.
Well, people could probably see that I wasn't --
Yeah, that's right.
